title: I'm not sure I believe anymore
seoTitle: Doubting Your Faith: Honest Help When You're Not Sure
description: Doubting your faith or wondering if God is real? Honest help from a pastor who came to faith from atheism: what doubt is, what it isn't, and what to do next.
summary: When the questions won't stop or God has gone quiet: doubt named honestly, and small steps to take this week.
askedAs: how do I know Christianity is true
I want to believe but I can't
is it a sin to doubt God
what does the Bible say about doubt
answer: You used to be sure, or sure enough, and now you're not. Maybe it came as one question nobody could answer, or a slow quiet where God used to be, or something the church did that made the whole thing hard to trust. You may still pray at night without knowing whether anyone is listening, and wonder whether that makes you a fraud. It doesn't. Doubt is not the same thing as unbelief, and some of the most honest people in the Bible said out loud what you're feeling. When they said it to Jesus, he didn't send them away. You don't have to settle this tonight. What you can do is smaller: name the real question, tell one person who won't panic, and keep bringing it to God, even if your only prayer is *I don't know if you're there*.
happening:
Doubt rarely arrives as a decision. It comes in pieces: a worship song you can't sing anymore without feeling like a liar, prayers that seem to stop at the ceiling, a question nobody at church ever answered, a prayer at a hospital bed that went unanswered, a leader you trusted who turned out to be someone else. Underneath it there's usually fear: of what your family will think, of losing your church, of what this means for your marriage or your kids, sometimes of hell itself. And there's the loneliness. You can't say it at church, and you're not sure you want to say it to the friends who have already left.

You've probably heard two explanations, from opposite directions. The first comes from church: doubt is sin or weakness, and the cure is to pray more, read more, and stop asking. There's something true in that. Faith does thin out when prayer, Scripture, and worship drop out of a life. But it can't account for the doubters the Bible makes room for, and it ignores how often the church produced the doubt by handing people answers too small for real life.

The second comes from the culture and from friends who have left: you're finally thinking for yourself. There's truth there too. Some of what you were handed deserves to fall, like a God who guarantees prosperity or a Christianity fused to a political party. But whether the scaffolding was bad and whether the building is true are different questions. And this explanation assumes every doubt is a conclusion reached by reason, when much of it is grief, exhaustion, or betrayal speaking in the voice of an argument.

Medicine and psychology offer a third explanation. Depression, grief, and plain exhaustion can drain the felt sense of God out of a life, so *I don't feel God anymore* may be telling you about your sleep or your sorrow before it tells you anything about God. If the flatness has spread to everything you used to love, see a doctor. Still, your questions aren't only symptoms, and the real ones deserve real answers.

So notice which kind of doubt you're carrying. Some of it is about truth: *is any of this real?* Some of it is felt: *I used to sense God, and now there's nothing.* And some of it is grief or anger dressed as a question: *how could a good God let this happen?* Most people carry a mix, and it matters which is loudest, because a reading list won't heal grief, and a hug won't tell you whether Jesus rose from the dead.

scripture.intro: The Bible doesn't hide its doubters. It names them, quotes them, and sometimes lets them speak a long time before God answers. These passages won't settle anything in a paragraph, and they aren't here to scold you out of your questions. They show how God has treated people standing where you stand: a father who couldn't quite believe, a worship leader whose faith nearly slipped, a disciple who asked for evidence, and followers who worshiped and doubted on the same mountain.

passages.text: Jesus asked the boy’s father, “How long has this been with him?” “From childhood,” he said. “It often throws him into the fire or into the water, trying to kill him. But if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” “If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!” Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”
passages.reading: Jesus has just come down from the mountain of the transfiguration into an argument: his other disciples have tried to help this boy and failed. The father has watched his son suffer since childhood and has just seen Jesus's own followers come up empty, so his “if You can” is what years of disappointment sound like. Jesus throws the *if* back at him, and the father answers with the most honest sentence in the chapter: he believes, and he needs help with the part of him that doesn't. Jesus takes the half-belief as it is and heals the boy. Later he tells the disciples this kind comes out only by prayer (Mark 9:29), and the only one in the scene who asked him for help was a father who couldn't quite believe. A divided heart, turned toward Jesus, can still pray.

passages.text: But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled; my steps had nearly slipped. For I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. ... Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands. ... When I tried to understand all this, it was troublesome in my sight until I entered God’s sanctuary; then I discerned their end. ... When my heart was grieved and I was pierced within, I was senseless and ignorant; I was a brute beast before You. Yet I am always with You; You hold my right hand.
passages.reading: The psalm is credited to Asaph. That was the name of the Levite David put over the singers before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:4-5), and later of a whole family of temple singers who carried his name (Ezra 2:41), so whoever first prayed it, this is a worship leader's account of nearly losing his faith. It opens with a confession, that God is good to the pure in heart, and then admits the world didn't look like it. The arrogant prospered, and his own faithfulness looked like a waste. What turned him was a place: he went into God's sanctuary and saw the story from its end. Then he confesses that he had been senseless, a brute beast before God, and that all the while God was holding his right hand. The grip was never his. And this psalm opens the third book of the Psalter: God's people kept a near-collapse of faith in their songbook and sang it.

passages.text: Now Thomas called Didymus, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus came. So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replied, “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” Eight days later, His disciples were once again inside with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” Then Jesus said to Thomas, “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” Thomas replied, “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”
passages.reading: Thomas missed the first Easter evening, so he was asked to believe the most unlikely claim in the world on his friends' word. This is the same disciple who, when Jesus turned back toward Judea where he had nearly been stoned, told the others, “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him” (John 11:16). He was brave, and he wanted what the others had been given. Eight days later Jesus came back, spoke peace first, and offered Thomas the evidence he had demanded, in Thomas's own words. John's Gospel opens by saying the Word was God (John 1:1), and the one who finally says so to Jesus's face is the doubter. Then Jesus turns to all who would never see what Thomas saw, and John adds that he wrote his book “so that you may believe” (John 20:31). He wrote it for every Thomas who wasn't in the room.

passages.text: Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted. Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”
passages.reading: This is the last scene of Matthew's Gospel, and Matthew could have left one detail out: they worshiped, but some doubted. He used the same word earlier for Peter sinking in the waves, when Jesus caught him first and only then asked, “why did you doubt?” (Matthew 14:31). It is a word for hesitation, a mind pulled two ways. And Jesus comes to this worshiping, wavering company without first sorting the sure from the unsure. He gives the whole group the commission, doubters included, and ends with a promise. The church was sent into the world from a mountain where worship and doubt stood side by side, and what it carried down that mountain was not its own certainty. It was his presence, to the end of the age.

whyHard:
Some of the weight you're carrying belongs to the age. The philosopher Charles Taylor spent a long book, *A Secular Age* (2007), asking how the West moved from a world around 1500 in which it was almost impossible not to believe in God to one in which belief is one option among several, and for many people not the obvious one. He argued against what he called subtraction stories, the tidy account in which science and reason simply stripped belief away and left the plain truth standing. What changed, in his account, was the setting of belief itself. You live beside kind, thoughtful people who believe something else or nothing at all, and you can explain most of your day without mentioning God, so even a committed believer feels faith as a choice that could be unmade. Asaph asked whether God was fair in a world that took God's existence for granted. You live where both questions hang in the air, and part of what you feel is the weather, not only the evidence.

Then there is the faith many of us were handed. It came as a set of answers, and questions were treated as disloyalty. I'm a pastor, and this indictment includes me. We have too often met a teenager's honest question with a verse and a warning, and treated the one who kept asking as a problem to manage. We answered grief with arguments and arguments with *just have faith*, until people concluded there was no answer at all. A faith that has never been allowed a question has never been tested, so when the first real one arrives, at a graveside or in a college classroom, it can feel like the first crack in a dam.

For some of you it started with a person: a pastor who fell, a leader who covered for someone, a church that was cruel to you or to someone you love. When the people who taught you about God are the ones who hurt you, the message becomes very hard to separate from the messenger, and that is no failure of intelligence. The church has earned much of the distrust aimed at it, and Jesus saved his hardest words for religious leaders who made faith harder for others: “You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces” (Matthew 23:13). For others it started further back. If your father was absent or cold, God's silence can sound like an old silence, and the word Father is hard to hear without hearing him. Either way, what happened to you is real evidence about the people involved. Whether Jesus is who he said he was is a separate question, and it deserves its own hearing.

I came to faith from atheism, so I won't pretend the objections are stupid or that the people who hold them are dishonest. Many of the objections are serious, and some of the people raising them are more honest than the churches that failed them. But honesty runs in more than one direction. It's honest to say you don't know. It's just as honest to keep looking, to read the strongest case beside the strongest objection, and to ask your question in the open, with people who can bear it and before the God it's about. Doubt kept in the dark tends to harden into a conclusion nobody examined. The question was never the danger. Being alone with it was.

thisWeek.intro: None of this asks you to decide anything by Sunday. These are small, honest things a person can do while still unsure. Start with the first one tonight, and take the rest as the week allows.

steps.title: Write down the real question
steps.body: Get it out of your head and onto paper, as plainly as you can. *I don't know if the resurrection happened* is a different question from *I haven't felt God since my dad died*, and both differ from *I can't trust anything my old church taught me*. Then ask which kind yours is. A named question is one you can take somewhere.

steps.title: Pray the honest prayer
steps.body: You don't have to feel anything or be sure of anything to pray. *I don't know if you're there*, said out loud or written in a notebook, is still a prayer. Psalm 88 ends in darkness with no resolution, and it's in the Bible. If you don't believe right now, you can still say the most honest sentence you have: *if you're there, I want to know*.

steps.title: Tell one honest person
steps.body: Choose someone who won't panic, preach, or cheer you out the door: a pastor you trust, a steady friend, a counselor. Say it plainly: *I'm not sure I believe anymore, and I don't want to pretend.* You aren't asking them to fix it. You're asking not to carry it alone. If there's no one in your church you could say that to, that tells you something about the church, and nothing yet about God.

steps.title: Read one Gospel slowly
steps.body: [The Gospel of Mark](/study/bible/mark/1) is the shortest of the four, and a chapter a day takes a little over two weeks. Read it as if you'd never heard it, and note what Jesus actually says and does, especially what surprises you. Luke says he investigated everything carefully and wrote “so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:4). Read it as testimony to be weighed.

steps.title: Stay near worship without pretending
steps.body: If you can go to church honestly, go, and sit in the back if that helps. You don't have to sing a line you can't mean; let the people around you carry the words for a while. Asaph's faith turned in the sanctuary (Psalm 73:17). If church is where you were hurt, this may mean a different congregation for now, or a quiet morning with the Psalms. What matters is staying within reach.

steps.title: Read the best case and the best objection
steps.body: Don't settle this against a strawman in either direction. [Did the Resurrection Actually Happen?](/writing/did-the-resurrection-happen) lays out the historical case, weighs the skeptical alternatives, and admits it isn't proof. [What the New Atheists Got Right](/writing/what-new-atheists-got-right) states the four leading New Atheists at full strength and concedes what they got right before it answers them. Both essays are written from inside the faith, so read the critics in their own words too. If you'd rather argue than read, [Test the Case](/tools/test-the-case) lets you push back at every step. Take your time. The truth will keep.

moreHelp.body:
Most doubt calls for honest reading, prayer, and good conversation, and a pastor can walk with you through it. Sometimes, though, doubt travels with depression, trauma, or a fear that won't let go, and then it's wise to bring in a doctor or a licensed counselor alongside your pastor. That doesn't mean your faith failed. You are a body and a soul at once, and both can need care.

To find a counselor, ask your doctor for a referral, check your insurance company's directory, or ask a pastor who knows which local counselors are good. If you want a Christian counselor, look for one who will neither push you out of your faith nor rush you back into certainty. Christian or not, make sure they're licensed in your state; your state's licensing board can confirm it. If a church hurt you, ask whether they have experience with spiritual abuse.

If the doubt has turned into not wanting to be alive, don't wait for an appointment. Call or text 988 at any hour, or go to the nearest emergency room.
signs: You've had thoughts of not wanting to be alive. Call or text 988 now.
The flatness has spread past God to sleep, food, work, and the people you love, for two weeks or more.
A fear that you've committed an unforgivable sin won't let go, no matter what you read or hear.
Walking into a church, or hearing certain songs or phrases, brings panic, shaking, or dread.
A pastor or church leader abused you or someone else. Tell a counselor, and report any crime, and any harm to a child, to the police or child protective services.
The question has split your marriage or family into sides, and every conversation becomes a fight.
moreHelp.firstCall: You can keep the first call simple: *I'm going through a crisis of faith, and it's affecting my sleep, my mood, and my family. I want someone who will take both my questions and my faith seriously.* Ask whether they're licensed in your state and whether they've worked with faith questions or church hurt. If you're calling your doctor, say plainly what has changed in your sleep, appetite, energy, and mood, and for how long.
moreHelp.cost: Cost shouldn't keep you from help. Ask any counselor about a sliding scale based on income. Community mental health centers and university training clinics usually charge less, and many employers offer a few free sessions through an employee assistance program. Many churches keep a benevolence fund for needs like this, so ask. And a pastor's time costs you nothing.

helping.body:
If someone you love tells you they aren't sure they believe anymore, the first thing they need from you is evidence that telling you was safe. Your fear makes sense, especially if you're a parent, but fear makes us talk too fast, and a person met with panic learns to stop talking. Listen long enough to hear which kind of doubt it is: a question about truth, a silence they can't explain, or a wound. Only the first is helped much by a book.

Keep the relationship ordinary, and if they ask something you can't answer, say so and offer to look for the answer together. Jude wrote one of the sternest letters in the New Testament, but when he turned to the church's own wavering members, his instruction was to “have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 1:22).

I have five sons, and I would rather they bring me their hardest question than hide it to keep the peace. A home or a church where doubt can be said out loud is safer for faith. If you're a pastor, the person across from you may be doing the most honest thing they've done in years, and they're watching to see whether honesty and belonging can live in the same room.
say: Thank you for telling me. That took courage.
Nothing you say about this will make me love you less.
What's the question underneath all of it?
I don't know. Can we look for the answer together?
Do you want me to talk tonight, or just listen?
dontSay: Who have you been listening to?
Everyone goes through this. You'll get over it.
helping.next: Pray for them, and don't turn your prayers into messages they're meant to overhear. Offer to read a Gospel together, a chapter at a time, with no agenda beyond reading it. If you're out of your depth, bring in a pastor you both trust, with their permission. If they mention not wanting to be alive, stay with them and call or text 988 together. Then give it time. You aren't responsible for how their story ends, only for being someone they can keep telling it to.

prayer:
God, if you are there, I don't know how to talk to you anymore. I used to be sure, or I thought I was, and I'm tired of pretending. You know which part of this is a question and which part is grief, and I'm not sure I do.

You didn't send away the father who couldn't quite believe. You let Thomas ask to see your hands. So I'm asking. Show me what is true, even if it costs me. Keep me from lying to the people who love me, or to myself, in either direction. If the faith I was handed was smaller than you are, don't let me throw you out with it. And if I'm the one who has been wrong, give me the courage to see it.

I can't hold on very well right now. Asaph said you held his right hand when he was too senseless to hold yours. Hold mine, whether I can feel it or not.

I believe a little. Help the rest of me. Amen.

faq.q: Is it a sin to doubt God?
faq.a: Doubt isn't the same as unbelief. The unbelief Hebrews warns against is a heart that turns away from the living God (Hebrews 3:12); doubt is a mind pulled two ways, still partly facing him. Faithful people doubt all through the Bible, and God meets them there; even John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask Jesus whether he was the one (Matthew 11:3). People often cite the letter of James, which compares a doubter to a wave tossed by the wind (James 1:6). The same letter calls that person double-minded (James 1:8), the word it also uses for people trying to love God and the world at once (James 4:4-8), so many readers take the warning to be about divided loyalty, a heart hedging its bets, rather than an honest question. Others read it as a rebuke to any wavering in prayer. Either way, the passage opens with an invitation to ask God, “who gives generously to all without finding fault” (James 1:5). A hard question brought to God is still a way of facing him.

faq.q: How do I know if Christianity is true?
faq.a: No argument gives mathematical certainty, and anyone who promises it is overselling. But Christianity stakes everything on a historical event, and Paul said so bluntly: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). That moves the question from feelings and upbringing to what happened outside Jerusalem one Passover weekend around AD 30. Read one Gospel slowly, then weigh the case for the resurrection against the strongest objections, as you would any serious claim about the past. The Skeptic's Track on this site takes the resurrection and the other hard questions in order, in essays written for skeptics first. You deserve to reach your verdict honestly, and you don't have to reach it quickly.

faq.q: Why don't I feel God anymore?
faq.a: The felt sense of God's nearness comes and goes, even for people whose faith is steady, and its absence doesn't prove that God is absent. In the sixteenth century John of the Cross wrote of a dark night when prayer goes dry, and he likened it to a mother weaning her child and setting it down to walk. The Psalms pray straight into that silence: “Why do You hide Your face from me?” (Psalm 88:14). Be honest about your body too, since grief, depression, and exhaustion can flatten every feeling; if the numbness has spread to everything, see a doctor. Meanwhile, keep praying honestly, even when all you can say is that you don't know whether he's there.

faq.q: Is deconstruction the same as losing my faith?
faq.a: It doesn't have to be. Deconstruction usually means taking an inherited faith apart to see which pieces bear weight, and much of what gets examined deserves it: faith fused to a political tribe, promises of prosperity God never made, a church that treated every question as rebellion. Some people take it all apart and walk away. Others find something older underneath: the Jesus of the Gospels, whom no party owns, and the faith the church has confessed in its creeds for centuries. Honest questioning doesn't have to stop at the rubble. It can keep digging until it reaches what is older and truer than what fell.

faq.q: What if my doubts started with something the church did?
faq.a: Then your doubt has a real cause and deserves to be taken seriously. When pastors lie, leaders cover up abuse, or a congregation is cruel, the damage reaches past them to the God they claimed to speak for. Jesus was hardest on religious leaders who blocked the way for others (Matthew 23:13). It helps to pull apart two questions that got fused: whether that church was trustworthy, and whether Jesus is who he said he was. The second deserves its own hearing. If you were abused, you don't have to go back, and you should tell someone who can help, including the police when a crime was committed.

slots.note: James's own account of coming to faith from atheism, only if he chooses to write it: what he believed and doubted as an atheist, what kept him out, and what finally moved him, told for a reader who may be walking the other direction. It would sit with the paragraph that begins with his coming to faith from atheism; the page stands without it.
Whether growing up without a father shaped how James heard the word Father when he came to faith, in his own words, beside the sentence about God's silence sounding like an old silence.
As a father of five sons, what James would want a parent to hear when a child says they don't believe anymore, in his own words and without describing his sons' private faith.

reviewed.notes: Second-pass edit, done in full from the top. Validator clean (node scripts/validate-needs.mjs doubt). Truth: Charles Taylor's A Secular Age (2007), its question about belief around 1500 and its case against subtraction stories; John of the Cross, Dark Night, Book I, chapter 1 (the mother who weans her child and sets it down to walk); and Britannica's dating of the crucifixion (Passover, between AD 29 and 33, possibly 30) were each confirmed as the page characterizes them, and each source URL confirmed to exist, through search-engine excerpts, because the source sites are blocked from this environment; re-open each before release. Matthew uses the same verb for doubt in 14:31 and 28:17 (distazo, which occurs only in those two verses in the New Testament): confirmed and kept. Every reading rechecked in context with scripts/bsb.mjs: Mark 9:2 and 9:14-29; Psalm 73 with 1 Chronicles 16:4-7 and Ezra 2:41; John 1:1, 11:7-16, and 20:19-31; Matthew 11:2-6, 14:28-33, 23:13, and 28:16-20; Jude 1:17-23; Luke 1:1-4; Psalm 88; Hebrews 3:12; James 1:5-8 and 4:4-8; 1 Corinthians 15:14-17. Changes: the answer now says that those who brought their doubt to Jesus were not sent away (it had extended that to psalmists who never met him); the FAQ on James 1:6-8 presents divided loyalty as one reading, states the other (a rebuke to any wavering in prayer) fairly, and adds the passage's own opening invitation (James 1:5); the deconstruction FAQ commits instead of hedging with I don't think and drops a second stacked triplet; a mixed metaphor in whyHard repaired. No sentence says James says or wrote about the New Testament letter (it is the letter of James throughout); James is described only as a pastor, and nothing speaks for a denomination or tradition. Related already carries the starter needs deconstructing, church-hurt, and curious. Every kit label checked against its target (plans-index, the study guide index, the essay titles in the static library and content-data, the pathway, wisdom, and how-to manifests, and the page components): doubt has no eight-week plan of its own, so the kit uses the deconstruction plan under its real title. No statistics, no quotations but Scripture, no biography beyond the approved facts, first person only for conviction; the 988 lines follow safe-messaging language. Read as the person at midnight on a phone, the skeptic, the pastor, and a licensed counselor.
